# Few-Step Distilled Video: Time & Cost per Clip on H100

 Connor Blier Founding GTM 

 

 On an H100, the time and cost per clip for diffusion video scale almost linearly with denoising steps. Few-step distillation cuts the step count, not the GPU price: drop from 40 steps to 6-8 and you cut per-clip wall-clock and spend by roughly the same factor, around 5x.

...

```
time_per_clip  ≈ steps × time_per_step
cost_per_clip  ≈ time_per_clip × gpu_cost_per_second

...

The GPU is fixed the moment you pick an H100. `time_per_step` is fixed by the model, resolution and clip length. That leaves `steps` as the one term you can cut without changing hardware or buying a bigger box. Few-step distillation is the technique that cuts it, and it is why step count - not hourly rate - is the lever worth most of your attention.

...

## How to estimate cost per clip on an H100

Serverless GPU platforms bill per second, so cost per clip is just time per clip times the per-second rate. Our published per-GPU-second table puts the H100 at roughly $0.000953 per second on Cerebrium:

```
cost_per_clip ≈ time_per_clip × $0.000953
```

But the number that should drive your decision is cost per usable clip, not cost per generation. Video has a reroll problem: if a share of outputs are unusable, your effective cost is higher than the sticker. We work through that framing in Sora API alternatives: text-to-video cost per clip. The relevance to distillation is direct - a 5x cheaper clip that you have to reroll twice as often has only cut your real cost by about 2.5x. Track acceptance rate alongside step count.

...

The GPU rate is roughly fixed and serious providers cluster within about 30% of each other. Step count is the term you fully control, and a 5x step reduction beats any realistic swap in hourly rate.

# Local FastAPI to Serverless GPU Endpoint: Migration Guide

 Connor Blier Founding GTM 

 

 Local FastAPI to Serverless GPU Endpoint: Migration Guide 

 Moving from a local FastAPI model server to a serverless GPU endpoint rarely means rewriting your model code. The real work is relocating startup, taming cold starts and model-weight loading, and re-architecting for scale-to-zero billing. Your handler logic mostly survives the move intact.

...

## Choosing a serverless GPU platform

Don't start from a price table. As Northflank advises, "Compare the execution model before comparing the price" (Northflank). Evaluate against your workload:

- Deployment model. Do you ship a container and own the runtime, or hand over a model name? RunPod lets you "deploy any containerized model as an autoscaling GPU endpoint," while Modal lets you define GPU requirements "right in line with application code."
- Cold-start behaviour. Scale-to-zero only pays off if scale-up is fast. Vendors range widely in claimed starts.
- Billing granularity. Per-second billing is common; Northflank lists an H100 80GB at "$2.74/hour" and Modal's H100 component at "approximately $3.95/hour." For reference, Cerebrium's own CPU rate is $0.000026 per second.

results.title: Serverless vs Always-On GPU: LLM Break-Even | Cerebrium
results.author: Connor Blier
highlights:
Serverless vs Always-On GPU: LLM Break-Even | Cerebrium

- Nov 4, 2026 

# Serverless vs Always-On GPU: LLM Break-Even

 Connor Blier Founding GTM 

 

 Serverless vs Always-On GPU: LLM Break-Even 

 For LLM inference, an always-on GPU becomes cheaper than serverless once your workers would be billed for more than roughly 29 minutes per hour, about 48% utilization, on a RunPod A40. Below that line serverless scale-to-zero wins; above it the always-on pod does. The crossover shifts with concurrency, model size, and how billed time is counted. 

## The short answer

Serverless GPUs bill you only while a worker is running, so they win when your traffic is bursty and your hardware would otherwise sit idle. Always-on GPUs bill continuously, so they win once you keep the accelerator busy enough to amortize the idle hours. On a RunPod A40, the crossover sits at roughly 29 minutes of billed time per hour (about 48% utilization) - below it serverless is cheaper, above it an always-on pod is. When both are fully saturated, the same benchmark found a busy serverless worker costs about 2.3x more per token than a pod on identical hardware.

That premium is the price of elasticity. The question for a CTO is not "which is cheaper" in the abstract - it is "what is my steady-state utilization, and does it sit above or below the break-even line."

## The break-even formula

Every comparison reduces to cost per 1M tokens:

```
$ per 1M tokens = hourly GPU price / (tokens per second x 3600) x 1,000,000
```

The numerator is what you pay; the denominator is what you produce. For an always-on pod the hourly price is fixed whether or not requests arrive, so your effective cost per token is only as low as your busy utilization allows. For serverless, you pay the (higher) per-second rate but only for billed utilization - the fraction of the hour a worker is actually spun up.

...

So the decision rule is blunt: if a single GPU's worth of your traffic keeps that GPU busy more than half the hour, rent it always-on. If your traffic is spikier than that - a few busy minutes, then quiet - serverless scale-to-zero wins despite the per-token premium. For a larger-model version of this same crossover, see Llama 405B serverless GPU inference cost.

## GPU hourly rates to plug in

The numerator is just a number you look up. Recent on-demand rates (Runcrate, October 2026):

| GPU | VRAM | Region | On-demand $/hr |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RTX A6000 | 48 GB | Des Moines, US | $0.74 |
| L40S | 48 GB | Kansas City, US | $1.14 |
| H100 PCIe | 80 GB | Montreal, CA | $3.55 |

A cheaper card is not automatically the cheaper token. The H100 costs nearly 5x the A6000 per hour, but if it produces more than 5x the tokens per second for your model, it wins on cost per token. That is why the denominator - throughput - usually decides, and throughput is dominated by concurrency.

## The concurrency cost curve

Here is the part that quietly moves the break-even line. The same hardware gets dramatically cheaper per token as you batch more concurrent requests onto it. From a vLLM benchmark of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the RTX A6000:

| Concurrency | Tokens/sec | $ per 1M tokens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 42 | $4.86 |
| 8 | 307 | $0.67 |
| 32 | 1,012 | $0.20 |

Serving one request at a time, the A6000 managed 42 tokens/sec at $4.86 per 1M tokens. At concurrency 8 it hit 307 tokens/sec and $0.67. At concurrency 32 it reached 1,012 tokens/sec and just $0.20 - a 24x drop in per-token cost from the same GPU, purely from batching.

This reshapes the break-even. High concurrency lowers your always-on cost per token, which pushes the crossover down - an always-on pod running near saturation is very hard for serverless to beat. But it also raises the bar for keeping that pod fed: you need enough steady traffic to sustain concurrency 32, or the throughput (and the cheap token price) evaporates. The deeper treatment of batching economics lives in LLM inference cost at scale.

# Batch vs Real-Time LLM Inference Cost Per Million Tokens

 Connor Blier Founding GTM 

 

 Batch vs Real-Time LLM Inference Cost Per Million Tokens 

 Batch LLM inference is typically 2-3x cheaper per million tokens than real-time, because batch runs on busy, fully-utilized workers at a discounted tier. Real-time pays a premium for idle, scale-to-zero capacity. The pivot is utilization: real-time only wins when workers sit mostly idle. 

## The one-line answer

Batch is the cheaper tier for cost per million tokens whenever your work can wait, because batch requests run on fully-busy workers and are billed at a discount, while real-time pays a premium to keep latency-sensitive capacity on standby. On Runpod, batch requests are billed at up to 30% off on-demand pricing (20% off on H100, H200, B200 and B300). Real-time serverless, by contrast, can cost about 2.3x as much per token as a persistent pod on the same GPU when the worker stays busy. So the question `batch vs real time llm inference cost per million tokens` is really a question about one number: how busy your workers are.

...

The trap is reading provider price pages as if cost per million tokens were fixed. It is not. Cost per token is the hourly GPU rate divided by tokens produced in that hour, and tokens produced depends entirely on batch size and how continuously the worker runs. We worked the full chain through in our LLM inference cost at scale guide, and the per-request version in token usage and cost-per-request tracking.

...

## The batch discount: batch is a distinct pricing tier

Batch is not just "real-time, slower." It is a separate economic product. Batch and long-context are now tracked as distinct pricing modes in LLM API pricing datasets, alongside caching - which is the market's way of saying the per-token rate genuinely differs.

The discount is explicit on self-hosted-style platforms too: Runpod's batch requests are billed at 20% off on H100, H200, B200 and B300, and up to 30% off depending on GPU type. Stack that stated discount on top of the higher batch-size throughput above and you get the familiar 2-3x gap for offline workloads: embeddings, document enrichment, evals, and synthetic data generation. For transcription, we break the same math down per audio-hour in Whisper batch transcription cost.

...

Here is the pivot the sticker prices hide. Runpod found Serverless costs less than Pods only when its flex workers would be billed for under about 29 minutes of each hour. That is the line. Below roughly 48% utilization, elastic real-time wins because you stop paying for idle. Above it, a persistent pod - or a batch tier - is cheaper, because you are paying the ~2.3x busy-worker premium on a worker that is almost always busy anyway.

...

- Worker busy < ~29 min/hour: real-time serverless with scale-to-zero is cheapest. Pay per request, not per idle minute.
- Worker busy > ~29 min/hour: you are effectively always-on. A persistent pod avoids the serverless premium, and a batch tier adds the explicit 20-30% discount on top.

...

results.author: Connor Blier
highlights:
Together AI Alternatives for Fine-Tuned LLM Inference

- Oct 16, 2026 

# Together AI Alternatives for Fine-Tuned LLM Inference

 Connor Blier Founding GTM 

 Together AI Alternatives for Fine-Tuned LLM Inference 

 The best Together AI alternatives for fine-tuned LLM inference fall into three archetypes: model APIs that serve fine-tunes (Fireworks, Predibase), managed serverless platforms (Baseten, Modal, Replicate, Cerebrium), and self-managed GPU (Anyscale). Choose by how you need to serve LoRA adapters, your billing unit, and deployment control.

...

1. Serverless fine-tuned inference. Can you serve a fine-tune without reserving a dedicated endpoint? Predibase's serverless fine-tuned endpoints let you "query their fine-tuned LLMs at the same exact per-token price as base models." Fireworks serves fine-tunes serverless with "no additional costs".
2. Multi-LoRA serving. If you run many adapters, you want dynamic loading rather than one endpoint per variant. Fireworks offers live merge vs multi-LoRA; Predibase's LoRAX does dynamic adapter loading, tiered caching, and continuous multi-adapter batching; Baseten uses LoRA swapping with TensorRT-LLM. We cover the pattern in running multiple models on one GPU.
3. Pricing model. Per-token (model APIs) hides the GPU; per-second or per-GPU-hour (managed serverless) exposes it but rewards efficiency. See LLM inference cost at scale.
4. Deployment control. Managed endpoint you cannot touch, versus your own container and framework. This is the axis where serverless GPU platforms win.

...

| Platform | Archetype | Fine-tune training | Multi-LoRA | Billing unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Together AI | Model API + tuning | Yes (LoRA/full) | Limited | Per token |
| Fireworks | Model API | Yes | Live merge / multi-LoRA | Per token |
| Predibase | Model API | Yes | LoRAX | Per token |
| Baseten | Managed serverless | Serve only | LoRA swap (TRT-LLM) | Per GPU-minute |
| Modal | Managed serverless | Yes (GPU attach) | Your code | Per second |
| Replicate | Managed serverless | Yes | Your code | Per second |
| Cerebrium | Managed serverless | Serve + train | Your code | Per second |
| Anyscale | Self-managed GPU | Yes (Ray) | Your code | Per GPU-hour |

...

This archetype replaces only the serving half - you own training - in exchange for control and efficiency. ... Modal attaches pay-as-you-go GPUs in a couple of lines and notes a fine-tuned Llama 7B can be "around 50 times" cheaper per token than GPT-3.5. Replicate serves custom models per-second.

Cerebrium sits here too, and here is where we can speak from first-hand data. In our benchmarks on 1xH100 at 256 input tokens, we measured a lowest TTFT of 123ms with vLLM and peak throughput of 460 tokens/sec with SGLang at batch size 64. For TensorRT-LLM, our Llama 3 8B deploy showed a ~10-15s cold start to load the model into GPU memory. And production economics hold up: DistilLabs cut inference costs 50% while raising accuracy from 83% to 92%. For the broader serverless comparison see our Modal alternatives, Baseten alternatives and Replicate alternatives guides.

...

## Pricing by billing unit

- Per token (Together, Fireworks, Predibase): simplest to forecast, but you pay a margin on top of GPU cost and cannot optimize the hardware. Best for spiky or low-volume traffic.
- Per second (Modal, Replicate, Cerebrium): you pay for exactly the compute you use, so batching and framework choice directly lower your bill.
- Per GPU-hour (Anyscale, dedicated endpoints): cheapest per unit at steady high utilization, most expensive when idle.

...

How do the pricing models differ?

Model APIs bill per token and hide the GPU. Managed serverless platforms like Modal and Cerebrium bill per second, so batching and framework choice lower your bill directly. Self-managed GPU bills per GPU-hour, cheapest at steady high utilization and most expensive when idle.

results.author: Connor Blier
highlights:
vLLM on TPU vs H100: Cost & Throughput Guide | Cerebrium

- Nov 2, 2026 

# vLLM on TPU vs H100: Cost & Throughput Guide

 Connor Blier Founding GTM 

 

 vLLM now runs natively on Google TPU through TorchTPU with full feature parity, so choosing between TPU and the H100 GPU is no longer a compatibility question but a cost-and-throughput buyer decision you should measure on your own workload using trusted first-hand GPU baselines as your reference point.

...

This guide frames that decision the way we'd run it internally: what actually changed on the TPU side, the orchestration layer that now spans both accelerators, the first-hand H100 vLLM numbers we've measured as a GPU baseline, and a framework you can run on your own traffic. One guardrail up front, because it matters for how you read this: there is no honest head-to-head TPU-vs-H100 cost table to publish yet. The concrete throughput, cold-start, and cost figures below are all GPU-side measurements. The TPU side is a capability story. Treat anyone selling you a clean "Nx cheaper" number with suspicion until they show you the workload it was measured on.

...

### Throughput

On Llama 3.1 70B FP8 on a single H100, in our testing SGLang was the throughput winner, "achieving a throughput of 460 tokens per second on a batch size of 64." On smaller models the per-card ceiling is higher: for Llama 3 8B we measured "~1700 output tokens per second (FP8) on a single Nvidia A10" (the A100 and H100 figures cited alongside it are NVIDIA's published TensorRT-LLM extrapolations, not ours). The headline: throughput is a function of model, engine, quantization, and batch size - not the card alone.

...

### Cost

Cost is where workload shape dominates. One customer running single-digit-million requests/day: "With Cerebrium, we reduced their inference costs by 50%, and increased accuracy from 83% to 92%, while keeping latency and reliability consistent at production scale." That gain came from serving architecture and autoscaling, not a different chip - a useful reminder that accelerator choice is one of several cost levers. For the full picture, see LLM inference cost at scale.

...

Is TPU cheaper than the H100 for LLM inference?

There's no honest universal answer, and we won't publish an invented one. Cost per million tokens depends on your model, quantization, batch size, context length, and SLO. Run the same vLLM workload on both targets, normalize to cost per million output tokens at a fixed latency SLO, and let your own numbers decide.

# 4-Bit LLM Inference on H100: Throughput, VRAM & Cost

 Connor Blier Founding GTM 

 

 4-bit LLM inference on the H100 is how you fit models that FP16 cannot, then serve them cheaply. Quantization makes 405B-class models runnable on 80GB cards, pushes throughput past a billion tokens per minute per H100, and drops cost to under six cents per billion tokens.

## Cost per token

Throughput is the lever, but cost per token is the number your CFO reads. Because a quantized model moves more tokens through the same rented H100, the cost of each token falls proportionally. With Quail on quantized models, H100 inference comes out to under 6 cents per billion tokens on Modal. For the full picture of how batching, utilization and idle time compound into your monthly bill, see our guide to LLM inference cost at scale.

...

## Deploy it on Cerebrium

Cerebrium runs quantized LLM inference on serverless H100s with per-second billing, fast cold starts and OpenAI-compatible endpoints - so you can serve a 4-bit or FP8 model, autoscale it, and pay only for the tokens you actually move. If you are comparing providers first, start with our Modal alternatives and Baseten alternatives breakdowns, then deploy.
